intuition.text: Of the subjects, this one remembers exactly one thing: the last value it was given. That makes it a state rather than a stream of news. Anyone who asks, by subscribing or by reading it directly, learns how things stand now and nothing about how they got there, and since it compares nothing, a repeated value is passed on as if it were new.
intuition.situation: A Play and Pause button whose label must say whether the scene is running, and a status panel that can be opened at any moment. The panel has to show the current status the instant it opens, not stay blank until someone next presses a button.

example.name: Play, Pause and a panel opened late
example.description: The status starts as {initial}. Play is pressed at frames 3 and 7 and Pause at frame 10, and each press pushes the status it sets into one BehaviorSubject; the second Play comes while the scene is already running. The button's label listens from frame 0 and the status panel subscribes at frame {panelOpensAt}, while the scene runs. In the app play() and pause() call next on the subject with true or false; here the presses are an input stream the subject subscribes to, and the status is named, {initial} or running, so the drawing can say it.

step0.title: Start with a value
step0.text: The subject cannot be made without one: the status is {initial} before anything is pressed, so a listener always has something to show.

step1.title: Give each new subscriber the held value at once
step1.text: Subscribing adds the listener to the list and, within the same call, hands it the value the subject holds. The button hears {initial} the moment it subscribes, and the panel subscribing at frame {panelOpensAt} hears running then, without waiting for the next press. A subject that has already completed or failed hands a newcomer only that ending, and no value.

step2.title: Keep the newest value and pass it on
step2.text: A pushed value replaces the one held and is then handed to every listener. Nothing is compared: the second Play sets running again, and both listeners hear it again.

step3.title: Answer a direct question
step3.text: Code can also read the held value without subscribing. It gets that value, even after completion, but the read fails once the subject has errored or been torn down.

pseudocode.ordinary:
status holds one value, given when it is made, and a list of listeners
status keeps nothing older than that value
connect status to the presses, once

when a part of the page starts listening to status:
  if status has ended: pass on that ending at once, and no value
  otherwise:
    add the listener to the list
    hand it the held value, at once

when a press pushes a value in:
  replace the held value with it
  hand it to every listener, even if it equals the last

when code reads the held value directly:
  if status ended with an error: fail with that error
  if status has been torn down: fail
  otherwise: answer the held value, even after completion

limits.item0: It keeps one value, not a history: the panel subscribing at frame {panelOpensAt} learns that the scene is running, not that it was {initial} before. For the last few values use a ReplaySubject with a bounded buffer; for a single value delivered when the work completes, an AsyncSubject.
limits.item1: It needs a value before there is one. When nothing sensible exists yet, an invented placeholder such as null or an empty list reaches every subscriber, and each must treat it as not yet known. A ReplaySubject with a buffer of one also hands late subscribers the latest value, but emits nothing until a real one arrives.
limits.item2: It passes on every value, equal or not: the second Play reaches both listeners again. When a repeat would restart work downstream, put distinctUntilChanged after it, as the scene clock does before its switchMap.
limits.item3: After it completes, a new subscriber hears only the completion and not the last value, although value still returns it. A status that can end is better kept in a ReplaySubject with a buffer of one, which replays the last value before the completion.
limits.item4: Reading value pulls the current value outside the stream: nothing tells the reader when it changes, so code that reads it at the wrong moment acts on a stale value, and the read throws once the subject has errored or been unsubscribed. Subscribe, or keep the state in a signal, and read value only at a moment the code controls, as the scene facade does when it seeds its scan.

item0.why: Subject is the memory below: it keeps no value, so a late subscriber hears nothing until the next one, which suits a stream of events rather than a state.

item1.why: ReplaySubject with a buffer of one is the near twin: it needs no initial value and still replays its last value after completion.

item2.why: distinctUntilChanged drops the repeats a BehaviorSubject passes on, as the scene clock does before switching its frames.

item3.why: Reading BehaviorSubject.value is the rule against pulling the value where a subscription would keep the reader current.

item4.why: toSignal turns a stream into a signal; a BehaviorSubject's value on subscribing is the synchronous first emission toSignal can require.

notes.0: The status starts as paused, and the button subscribes: it is handed paused at once, before anything is pressed.
notes.3: Play is pressed. The subject replaces paused with running and hands it to the button, its only listener so far.
notes.5: The panel opens and subscribes. It is handed the held status, running, at once: it does not wait for the next press, and it never learns that the scene was paused before.
notes.7: Play is pressed again. The status was already running, but the subject does not compare: both listeners hear running again.
notes.10: Pause is pressed. The subject replaces running with paused and hands it to both listeners in the same frame.

intuition.text: catchError is where a pipeline decides whether a failure is the end of the story. Everything before the error passes through unchanged; what changes is the ending. Two decisions sit with it: what the reader sees instead of the failure, which the selector chooses, and how much of the pipeline the failure may end, which its position chooses. The stream that failed is finished either way. catchError picks a successor; it does not repair the source.
intuition.situation: A departures board fed by a live connection. When the connection drops, a blank board or an error page helps nobody. The printed timetable is a fair stand-in, provided the board says it is no longer live.

example.name: A departures board that falls back to the timetable
example.description: The board subscribes to departures$, a live feed, which sends two updates, {updates}, at frames 1 and 4 and then fails at frame 7 with {failure}. The selector answers with timetable$, the printed timetable, which takes {readFrames} frames to read, and marks its one entry with the error's message. The board keeps showing a departure and says why it is no longer live.

step0.title: Pass the source through
step0.text: While departures$ runs, each update goes to the board unchanged. Until an error arrives, catchError adds nothing.

step1.title: Hand the error to the selector
step1.text: When departures$ fails with {failure}, the error goes no further. catchError calls the selector with it, and the selector builds the replacement from it: the timetable, marked with what went wrong. Then catchError lets go of the finished feed.

step2.title: Continue with the replacement
step2.text: catchError subscribes to the stream the selector returned, in the frame of the failure, and passes its values on as if they came from the source.

step3.title: End as the replacement ends
step3.text: When the replacement completes, the board completes. Had the replacement failed, its error would have reached the board: catchError does not catch an error from its own replacement.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each update from the source:
  pass it on

when the source fails with error:
  replacement = selector(error)
  stop listening to the source
  (the error itself goes no further)

start listening to replacement
on each value from replacement:
  pass it on

when replacement completes:
  complete the output
when replacement fails:
  fail the output with its error

limits.item0: Placement decides what survives. catchError ends the stream it is on: after the error, the output carries the replacement and then completes. If the board reconnected on a Refresh button, switchMapping each press to a new departures$, the catch would belong on that inner feed, where this app's commands put theirs. Placed after switchMap instead, the first lost feed would complete the whole pipeline, and the next press of Refresh would never be heard.
limits.item1: It can hide a failure. A replacement such as EMPTY, or a plain default value, looks downstream exactly like a quiet success. Keep the evidence in the replacement, as the timetable entry carries {failure} here; turn the error into a failure value, as this app's commands do; or record it and rethrow with throwError, as its HTTP interceptor does.
limits.item2: It does not resume the source. Whatever the feed would have sent after its error is lost, and the replacement starts from its own beginning. Returning the selector's second argument, caught, subscribes the source again, but at once and without limit, so a source that always fails loops. retry gives a count and a delay.
limits.item3: An error from the replacement, or one thrown inside the selector, is not caught by the same catchError: it reaches the output. A timetable that could not be read would fail the board. A fallback that can itself fail needs a catchError of its own.

item0.why: retry starts the failed source again, up to a count and after a delay, where catchError replaces it. The two are often combined: retry first, and catchError for what to show once the retries run out.

item1.why: catchError inside the inner flattening is the placement that keeps a long-lived stream alive, the one this app's commands use.

item2.why: catchError → EMPTY vs fallback value weighs a silent replacement against one that surfaces the failure, the choice the second limit describes.

item3.why: onErrorResumeNextWith moves on to the next source whether the first failed or completed, and never sees the error, where catchError's selector receives it and chooses.

item4.why: throwError is what a selector returns to record an error and still pass it on, as the HTTP interceptor does.

intuition.text: combineLatest answers the question of what is true now across sources that change on their own schedules. Picture one pigeonhole per input: a report replaces whatever its own hole held, and once no hole is empty, every report produces a fresh snapshot of all of them. It never asks a source for anything; it only remembers the last thing each one said, and forgets everything said before.
intuition.situation: A dashboard row that shows a task's worker state beside the budget it has left. Either may change at any moment, the row must always pair the newest of both, and it cannot be drawn until both have reported once. It is the wrong tool when every report matters, since a value replaced before the other sources have spoken never reaches a row.

example.name: A dashboard row from a worker and its budget
example.description: The worker reports {workerStates} at frames 1, 2, 6 and 12 and completes at frame 15. The budget reports {budgets} at frames 4 and 8 and completes at frame 10, while the worker is still running. The worker's first two reports arrive before the budget has said anything. Each row joins the worker's latest state with the budget's latest report.

step0.title: Listen to every input
step0.text: When the row is subscribed, combineLatest subscribes to each input in the order given and keeps one empty slot for each.

step1.title: Keep only each input's latest value
step1.text: A value replaces whatever its input's slot held. The worker's queued is replaced by reading before the budget has reported, so no row will ever show it.

step2.title: Wait until every slot is filled
step2.text: Until every input has reported once, nothing is sent and nothing signals the wait. The worker's state sits in its slot until the budget's first report at frame 4.

step3.title: Send the latest of each
step3.text: From then on, every value from any input sends a copy of all the slots, which map joins into the row. A budget change alone rebuilds the row with the worker's unchanged state.

step4.title: Finish when every input has
step4.text: A completed input leaves its last value in its slot, so the budget's final report stays in every later row. The row completes when the last input completes. The first error from any input errors the row and unsubscribes the others.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the row starts listening:
  keep an empty slot for each input
  start listening to each input, in order

on each value from an input:
  put the value in that input's slot
  (whatever the slot held before is forgotten)

  if any slot is still empty:
    send nothing yet

  otherwise:
    send the latest of every slot together
    (here: joined into the row)

when an input finishes:
  leave its last value in its slot
  if every input has finished:
    finish the row
if an input fails:
  fail the row and stop listening to the others

limits.item0: Nothing is sent until every input has reported, and nothing says so. Here the worker's first two reports wait for the budget; an input that never reports keeps the row blank for good, with no error. When the row should appear before a slow source has reported, give that input a starting value with startWith, as Angular's router does with its guards.
limits.item1: Before every input has reported, an input's earlier values are overwritten unseen: queued never reaches a row. combineLatest is the wrong tool when every report matters, such as for an activity log; keep the worker's own stream for that.
limits.item2: A completed input keeps its last value in every later combination. The budget has stopped reporting before the worker is done, yet the final row still shows the budget's last report. That is right only if a finished source's last value is still true.
limits.item3: An input that completes without a value means no combination can ever be built, so the row completes empty, but only once every other input has completed too. The API reference says the output completes at once, the moment the empty input completes; the 7.8.2 source instead waits for the other inputs. Until they complete, the row is silent and they stay subscribed.
limits.item4: One error ends everything. The first error from any input errors the row and unsubscribes the others, so one failing source blanks the whole row. Catch the error on each input that may fail and replace it with a value the row can show.
limits.item5: Inputs that change together produce glitches. If two inputs derive from one source, each change of the source sends once per input, and the first of those combinations pairs a new value with a stale one that never held at the same time. Derive both parts from one stream with map, or combine only inputs that are independent.
limits.item6: Synchronous inputs are subscribed one after another, and an input that sends all its values while being subscribed has finished before the next input is subscribed. Only its last value takes part in any combination.

item0.why: withLatestFrom is the choice when only one input should rebuild the row and the others are read as context: a new budget alone would then send nothing.

item1.why: zip pairs values by position, the first of each and then the second of each, rather than by latest.

item2.why: forkJoin is the choice when only each input's final value matters: it sends once, when every input has completed.

item3.why: combineLatestWith is the same combination written as an operator in a pipe, with the source as the first input.

item4.why: startWith gives an input a value at subscription, so combineLatest need not wait for it.

item5.why: combineLatestAll is the same combination when the inputs arrive as a stream of streams.

notes.0: Nothing has reported yet. combineLatest has subscribed to both inputs and keeps an empty slot for each.
notes.1: The worker reports queued. Its slot is filled, but the budget has not reported, so no row can be built.
notes.2: The worker moves on to reading, which replaces queued in its slot. The budget is still silent, so there is still no row, and nothing says why.
notes.4: The budget reports {{budget}}% left. Every slot is now filled, so the first row appears. It pairs the budget with reading; queued never reaches a row.
notes.6: The worker moves on to writing. The row pairs it with the budget's latest value, still {{budget}}% left.
notes.8: The budget falls to {{budget}}% left, and the row is rebuilt with the worker's unchanged state, writing.
notes.10: The budget completes. combineLatest keeps its last value, {{budget}}% left, and the row stays open: the worker is still running.
notes.12: The worker is done. The row pairs done with the {{budget}}% left that the completed budget left in its slot.
notes.15: The worker completes. Every input has now completed, so the row completes.

intuition.text: One thing at a time, in the order it was asked for. concatMap starts the work for the first value and makes every later value wait in line; the next piece of work begins only once the current one has completed, which can be well after it first answered. Nothing is dropped and nothing overtakes: the output is each value's results in full, one value after another.
intuition.situation: A shared album that places each photo when its upload finishes. The user adds three photos in the order they want them shown. If a small photo added second could finish uploading before a large one added first, the album would show them the wrong way round, so each upload has to finish before the next one begins.

example.name: Three photos uploaded to a shared album
example.description: The user adds three photos, {photos}, at frames 1, 3 and 5, and is done adding at frame 8. The server answers cat's upload {catUpload} frames after it starts, dog's after {dogUpload} and owl's after {owlUpload}, and each upload completes on the frame after its answer. cat is a large photo and dog a small one, so dog's quick upload has to wait for cat's. The mergeMap study runs these same uploads at once.

step0.title: Send a photo when nothing is uploading
step0.text: When the user adds a photo and no upload is running, its upload is prepared and sent at once.

step1.title: Queue a photo that arrives during an upload
step1.text: If an upload is running, the photo joins the back of the queue. Its upload is not prepared yet: the function that makes it runs only when the photo's turn comes, so whatever that function reads, it reads then rather than when the photo was added.

step2.title: Pass on each answer
step2.text: Whatever the running upload returns goes straight to the output as it arrives.

step3.title: Start the next upload only when this one completes
step3.text: The turn passes when the running upload completes, not when the server answers it. Only then is the oldest waiting photo's upload prepared and sent, which is why dog, whose upload is the quickest, still waits for cat's to finish.

step4.title: Stop everything on a failure
step4.text: If an upload fails, the failure goes to the output and everything ends there: the photos still in the queue are thrown away without being sent, and photos added later are no longer listened to.

step5.title: Finish when the user is done and the queue is empty
step5.text: The output completes only once the user has finished adding photos, no photo is waiting and the last upload has completed. A user who stops adding while uploads are still owed leaves the output open until they are done.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each photo the user adds:
  if no upload is running:
    prepare and start the upload for photo

  otherwise:
    put photo at the back of the queue
    (its upload is prepared only when its turn comes)

on each answer from the running upload:
  pass the answer on

when the running upload completes:
  (an answer alone does not end its turn)
  if the queue is not empty:
    take the oldest photo off the queue
    prepare and start the upload for it

if the running upload fails:
  pass the failure on
  throw the queue away, unsent
  stop listening for new photos

when the user is done adding, the queue is empty and no upload is running:
  complete the output

limits.item0: The queue has no ceiling. While photos arrive faster than uploads complete, each waits longer than the one before, nothing signals that the line is growing, and every photo in it is held in memory until its turn. When the order does not matter, let the uploads overlap with mergeMap and a cap; when only the newest value matters, as with an autosave, put a debounceTime in front so that a burst becomes one value.
limits.item1: An upload that answers but never completes holds the queue for ever. The turn passes on completion, so an inner stream that stays open after answering, such as one that goes on listening for the server's processing updates, leaves every later photo waiting, without an error. End such an inner with first(), take(1) or a timeout before concatMap sees it.
limits.item2: One failed upload ends all uploading. The error reaches the output, the photos waiting in the queue are discarded without being sent and photos added later are no longer heard, so the album silently stops filling. Catch inside the projection, upload(photo).pipe(catchError(...)), to keep the queue running and report the one failure.
limits.item3: Every value's work runs, including work whose answer is already stale. For a search, or a details panel that follows a selection, concatMap makes the reader wait for answers to questions nobody is asking any more before the current one even starts: use switchMap there. Work that is independent, like these uploads once each photo carries its own place, need not wait at all: use mergeMap.

item0.why: mergeMap runs these same uploads at once: the album fills sooner, but dog is stored before cat. Reach for it when the pieces of work are independent and the order they finish in does not matter.

item1.why: switchMap is the choice when only the newest value's answer matters and older work can be abandoned, such as a search box.

item2.why: exhaustMap is the choice when a value arriving during the work should be ignored rather than queued, such as a second click on a submit button.

item3.why: concatAll is the same one-at-a-time queue over a stream that already carries the inner streams, when there is nothing left to project.

item4.why: The concat strategy sets this queue beside the other flattening policies as a choice of concurrency, which helps when deciding between them rather than learning one.

item5.why: Ordered writes is the pattern this example is an instance of, with the guards it needs against an upload that never completes and a queue that grows.

item6.why: debounceTime in front of concatMap suits work where only the newest value matters, such as an autosave: it waits for a pause, so a burst of edits becomes one save instead of a queue.

intuition.text: One job at a time, with an engaged tone rather than a waiting line. A request that arrives while the job is running is turned away at the door: it is not held for later and it does not interrupt the job. What frees the line is the job completing, not its first answer, so a job that has replied but not yet finished still counts as busy. Nothing is remembered of the requests turned away; once free, the operator waits for the next one to arrive.
intuition.situation: A Save button that a person double-clicks, or presses again because nothing seemed to happen. The first press should save the form; a second save of the same form must not start alongside it, and the first must not be abandoned halfway.

example.name: A Save button pressed four times
example.description: The button is pressed four times, at frames 1, 3, 8 and 10, and each press carries the form's draft at that moment: {drafts}. The form closes at frame 11, which completes the presses. A save answers {answersAfter} frames after it starts and completes {completesAfter} frames after it starts. The second and fourth presses arrive while a save is running.

step0.title: Start a save when none is running
step0.text: When a press arrives and no save is running, call save with its draft and keep that save as the one running.

step1.title: Turn a press away while a save runs
step1.text: When a press arrives while a save is running, turn it away. save is never called for its draft, nothing waits in a queue, and the running save carries on untouched.

step2.title: Pass on what the running save delivers
step2.text: Each answer the running save returns goes straight to the output.

step3.title: Free the slot when the save completes
step3.text: The slot frees when the running save completes, not when it answers. The next press to arrive then starts a new save; presses turned away earlier are not brought back.

step4.title: Finish only when both are done
step4.text: The output completes once the presses have completed and no save is running. Presses that complete while a save runs leave the output open until that save completes.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each draft from the button:
  if no save is running:
    running = start saving the draft

  otherwise:
    turn the draft away
    (save is never called for it, and nothing is queued)

on each answer from the running save:
  pass the answer on

when the running save completes:
  running = none
  (the next press starts a new save; drafts turned away stay lost)

when the button has completed and no save is running:
  complete the output

limits.item0: A press turned away is a value lost. exhaustMap discards the draft along with the request, so if the form changed between two presses only the earlier draft is saved: in this example draft 2 and draft 4 are never saved, and draft 4 is what the form held when it closed. That fits a button whose presses all mean the same thing. Where every value must be kept, concatMap saves each in turn; where only the newest matters and the running job may be abandoned, switchMap does that.
limits.item1: A save that never completes locks the button. Every press is turned away until the running inner stream completes, so a request that hangs, or an inner stream that keeps listening for more, leaves the button dead for good. Bound the inner stream, for example with timeout or take, so that it always ends.
limits.item2: A failed save ends the whole output. An error from the inner stream reaches the output and terminates it, so later presses go nowhere. Catch the error inside the inner stream, as the NgRx sign-in effect does, so that a failure ends only its own attempt.
limits.item3: Turning a press away is silent. Nothing tells the person that the second press did nothing, so the screen should say it too: disable or mark the button while a save runs.

item0.why: switchMap makes the opposite choice: the newest value wins and cancels the one running. That suits a search, where a stale answer is worthless, and never a save.

item1.why: concatMap keeps every value and runs the inner streams one after another in order, the choice when each draft must be saved.

item2.why: mergeMap runs every inner stream at once, the choice when overlapping saves are harmless and the order of their answers does not matter.

item3.why: exhaustAll applies the same rule to a stream whose values are already streams, when the projection has been done elsewhere.

item4.why: throttle also ignores values for a while after one passes, but its quiet window is a duration it is given rather than the work itself, and the value passes through unprojected: it limits how often, where exhaustMap waits for a job to finish.

intuition.text: finalize ties a clean-up to the life of a subscription rather than to any message on it. Values pass untouched while it waits; it acts only when the subscription is over, and only after whatever ending there was has been passed on, so the code that hears that the stream is done runs before the code that tidies up after it.
intuition.situation: A spinner shown while a download runs. It must go when the download finishes and when it fails, and also when the reader leaves the page halfway and the view unsubscribes. Leaving sends no completion and no error, so only a clean-up tied to the subscription catches all three.

example.name: A download the reader abandons
example.description: The reader starts a download and the page shows a spinner. Two clean-ups are attached with finalize: releasing the connection, nearer the source, then hiding the spinner. After {partsShown} parts the reader leaves the page and the view unsubscribes from shown$. The download neither completes nor fails, so the view is told nothing, yet both clean-ups run at that moment, the connection's first.

step0.title: Note the clean-ups when subscribed
step0.text: When the view subscribes to shown$, each finalize subscribes to what is above it and adds its callback to the subscription's finalizers. Nothing runs yet, and every part passes through unchanged.

step1.title: End for any of three reasons
step1.text: The subscription ends when the download completes, when it fails, or when the view unsubscribes, as it does here when the reader leaves. The clean-ups are not told which.

step2.title: Tell the view what it is owed
step2.text: A completion or a failure is passed to the view before anything is cleaned up. An unsubscription tells the view nothing: it is the one that left.

step3.title: Tear down from the source outward
step3.text: The finalizers run in the order they were added: the download's own teardown, which cuts it off, then each clean-up in the order the pipe lists them. The connection is released before the spinner hides, and neither runs again.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the view starts listening:
  start listening to the download
  add each clean-up to the things to run at the end
  (pass every part through unchanged)

when the download completes or fails, or the view stops listening:
  stop listening to the download
  (the clean-ups are not told which of these it was)

if the end was a completion or a failure:
  pass it to the view first
otherwise:
  tell the view nothing

then run the things to run at the end, oldest first:
  the download's own clean-up, which cuts it off
  each clean-up, in the order they were attached

item0.supports: finalize calls its callback when the source completes or errors, and also when the subscriber explicitly unsubscribes.

item1.title: finalize.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version finalize subscribes the downstream subscriber to its source and only then adds the callback to that subscriber, so the callback is a finalizer added after the source's own teardown.

item2.title: RxJS guide · Glossary and semantics, Finalization
item2.supports: The glossary treats finalization as cleaning up a producer's resources, guaranteed on error, completion or unsubscription and always part of unsubscription without being the same thing, and places a completion, when there is one, before finalization.

item3.title: Subscription.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item3.supports: unsubscribe runs a subscription's finalizers in the order they were added, catching what each throws, and once all have run throws those errors together as an UnsubscriptionError.

item4.title: Subscriber.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item4.supports: A subscriber passes complete or error to its destination and only then unsubscribes, so the observer hears the end before any finalizer runs.

item5.title: CHANGELOG.md in RxJS 7.8.2
item5.supports: Under 7.0.0-beta.1 the changelog lists the fix that made finalize's callback run after the source observable is torn down.

item6.title: tap.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item6.supports: tap calls its unsubscribe handler only when the subscription ends without a completion or failure passing through it, and its finalize handler on every end.

item7.title: pending_tasks.ts in Angular v22.2.3
item7.supports: PendingTasks.add() adds a task that blocks the application's stability and returns the function that removes it.

limits.item0: The callback is not told why the subscription ended: completing, failing and being unsubscribed all look the same to it. To act on the reason, use tap's handlers, whose unsubscribe handler runs only when no completion or failure passed through the tap, or keep a flag as Angular's router does.
limits.item1: It runs after the view has heard a completion or a failure, so code in the view's complete handler still sees the spinner showing, and the callback cannot send anything more into the stream it is cleaning up after.
limits.item2: Where it sits in the pipe decides what it cleans up after. Above a retry or repeat it runs at the end of every attempt; below one it runs once, when the last attempt ends.
limits.item3: A clean-up that throws never reaches the view's error handler. RxJS gathers the error into an UnsubscriptionError and throws it at the code that ended the subscription, so keep clean-ups from throwing.
limits.item4: Pipeline order is RxJS 7's behaviour. Since 7.0.0-beta.1 the callback has run after its source is torn down; an RxJS 6 codebase being upgraded may rely on its clean-ups running in another order.

item0.why: tap's subscribe, unsubscribe and finalize handlers sit at the same boundary as finalize, and its unsubscribe handler is the way to tell a reader leaving from the source's own end.

item1.why: Complete is not cancellation: the abandoned download sends no completion, so a tap complete handler on it never fires, while finalize does.

item2.why: using makes a resource for each subscription and disposes of it when the subscription ends, for a clean-up that belongs to something the stream itself creates.

item3.why: switchMap's cut-off ends an inner stream by unsubscription; a finalize inside the inner stream is how it notices, as Angular's router does.

item4.why: takeUntil ends the subscription from inside the pipe instead of from the view: placed last, it completes the view and unsubscribes everything above it, so every finalize above it runs.

intuition.text: materialize puts every signal a stream sends into an envelope and sends the envelope as an ordinary value. A value, a failure and a completion all arrive as records that say which they were, so a failure stops being something that tears the stream down and becomes data that can be shown, stored, counted or compared.
intuition.situation: An import reads a spreadsheet row by row and may fail partway. Its log panel should list every row read and then, as one more line, the reason the import stopped, instead of losing its stream to the import's error.

example.name: An import that fails on its third row
example.description: import$ emits {rows} and then fails, because {reason}. The log panel reads it through materialize, so it receives a record of kind N for each row and then one of kind E carrying the reason, after which log$ completes rather than failing.

step0.title: Wrap each value
step0.text: Each row import$ emits leaves log$ as a record of kind N whose value is the row. The row itself is not changed, only carried.

step1.title: Wrap the ending, then complete
step1.text: When import$ fails, the failure leaves as a record of kind E carrying the reason, and log$ completes at the same moment. Had the import completed, a record of kind C would have left instead, also followed by completion. Either way log$ never fails: whatever reads it learns how the import ended from its last record.

item4.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission, a hash an error, a bar completion, and parentheses group events that happen in the same frame, as the failure record and the completion do here.

limits.item0: materialize records a failure; it does not recover from one. The import still stopped at its third row, and log$ completes there. To go on after a failure, put retry or catchError before materialize.
limits.item1: Once a stream is materialized, operators that react to errors and completion find nothing to react to: a catchError or retry placed after materialize never sees the failure, which is now a value. Put them before it, or restore the signals with dematerialize first.
limits.item2: In RxJS 7 each record is an instance of the Notification class, which also carries a deprecated hasValue flag. The class is to be removed in v8 and the docs recommend plain objects of the ObservableNotification shape, so code that reads the records should rely only on kind, value and error.
limits.item3: A record of kind E carries the error exactly as it was thrown. Stored or sent as JSON, an Error object comes out as an empty object, because its message is not an enumerable field; a log that must outlive the page should copy the message out first.

item0.why: Reach for dematerialize to turn the records back into values, an error and a completion once they have been handled as data, as NgRx does before dispatching.

item1.why: Type the records as ObservableNotification, the plain shape of a kind with a value or an error, whenever code reads or builds them.

item2.why: The Notification class is what RxJS 7 wraps each record in; read it to understand hasValue and its helpers, and build nothing new on it, since it is deprecated.

item3.why: Reach for toArray after materialize to keep a whole run, failure included, as one list to store or compare; toArray alone emits nothing when its source fails.

item4.why: Reach for catchError instead when a failure should be replaced by a fallback and the stream carry on, rather than kept as the stream's last record.

item5.why: Reach for tap instead when the signals only need watching, for logging, and the failure should still end the stream as an error.

item6.why: Reach for materialize with scan when a page shows the progress of work that may fail: the records fold into a status that survives the failure.

intuition.text: Everything at once, answers as they come. mergeMap starts the work for a value as soon as the value arrives, lets any number of those pieces of work run side by side, and passes on each result the moment it appears, so the output follows the order in which work finishes, not the order in which it was asked for. Given a cap as its second argument, it runs at most that many and makes the rest wait their turn.
intuition.situation: The same shared album, once each photo carries its own place, such as the date it was taken. The uploads are then independent and there is no reason for a small photo to wait behind a large one: all of them can run at once, the album is complete sooner, and each answer is matched to its photo by name, whatever order the answers come back in.

example.name: Three photos uploaded to a shared album
example.description: The user adds three photos, {photos}, at frames 1, 3 and 5, and is done adding at frame 8. The server answers cat's upload {catUpload} frames after it starts, dog's after {dogUpload} and owl's after {owlUpload}, and each upload completes on the frame after its answer. cat is a large photo and dog a small one, so dog's upload, started second, is answered first. The concatMap study runs these same uploads one at a time.

step0.title: Start every upload at once
step0.text: When the user adds a photo, its upload is prepared and started straight away, whatever else is running. Nothing waits: dog's upload begins while cat's is still going.

step1.title: Pass on each answer as it arrives
step1.text: Whichever upload the server answers first goes out first. The output keeps no note of which photo was added first, which is how dog's answer comes out ahead of cat's; the value itself has to say which photo it belongs to.

step2.title: Stop everything on a failure
step2.text: If any upload fails, the failure goes to the output, every other upload still running is cut off and photos added later are no longer listened to.

step3.title: Finish when the user is done and every upload has completed
step3.text: The output completes once the user has finished adding photos and no upload is still running. A user who stops adding while uploads are still going leaves the output open until the last of them completes.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each photo the user adds:
  prepare and start the upload for photo at once
  (uploads already running carry on beside it)

on each answer from any running upload:
  pass it on at once, whichever photo was added first

if any upload fails:
  pass the failure on
  cut off every other running upload
  stop listening for new photos

when the user is done adding and no upload is running:
  complete the output

limits.item0: Nothing limits how many run. Each photo starts uploading the moment it is added, so a user who drops two hundred photos opens two hundred uploads at once, and nothing in the stream pushes back. Pass a cap as the second argument, mergeMap((photo) => upload(photo), 3), and the rest wait in a queue; the queue itself has no ceiling, and a cap of one is concatMap.
limits.item1: Order is lost. Answers come out in the order the uploads finish, dog's before cat's here, so code that takes the latest answer to be the answer for the latest value is wrong: a search whose older query answers last overwrites the newer result. Keep the identity in the value, as each answer here names its photo; use concatMap when results must follow the order of the values, and switchMap when only the newest value's answer matters.
limits.item2: One failed upload fails them all. The error reaches the output, the other uploads still running are cut off part-way and photos added later are not heard. Catch inside the projection, upload(photo).pipe(catchError(() => of(failed))), so that one broken upload stays one broken upload.
limits.item3: An upload that never completes keeps the output open for ever, and under a cap it holds its slot for ever too, so with a cap of one everything behind it waits. An inner that goes on emitting, such as one that keeps listening for the server's processing updates, needs first(), take(1) or a timeout before it is merged.

item0.why: concatMap runs these same uploads one at a time: the album fills later, but in the order the photos were added. Reach for it when the order of the work matters.

item1.why: mergeAll is the same merging over a stream that already carries the inner streams, when nothing is left to project.

item2.why: The concurrent parameter is the cap this example leaves out, as it works across the operators that accept it; read it when choosing a cap, or to see why a cap of one is concatMap.

item3.why: Concurrency limits is the pattern for giving mergeMap a cap, with the ways a capped merge still fails: a backlog that grows and a stuck inner that keeps its slot.

item4.why: switchMap is the choice when only the newest value's answer matters and older work may be abandoned, such as a search box.

item5.why: exhaustMap is the choice when values that arrive during the work should be ignored rather than started, such as repeated clicks on a submit button.

item6.why: forkJoin is the choice when a fixed set of requests is known up front and the reader needs all of their answers together, once, rather than each as it lands.

item7.why: Catching inside the inner stream is how one failed upload stays one failed photo instead of ending them all.

intuition.text: Think of observeOn as a hand-off desk between the source and everything after it. The source keeps working at its own pace; what moves is the moment the next stage is told. Name animationFrameScheduler and the news waits for the browser's next paint; asapScheduler, for the code running now to finish; queueScheduler, for a delivery already under way to end. Nothing is merged or reordered at the desk: things are heard in the order they happened, only later.
intuition.situation: An upload's progress bar. The upload reports progress whenever the network does, sometimes twice between two paints of the screen, and its stream is not yours to change. Drawing the bar is only useful just before the browser paints, so you choose when the bar hears a report rather than when the upload makes one.

example.name: An upload that fails, heard at each paint
example.description: The upload reports {reports} at frames 1, 2 and 5, and fails at frame 6 with {failure}. The browser paints every {paintEvery} frames, starting at frame 3. The bar subscribes through observeOn(animationFrameScheduler), so it hears the reports only at a paint, and hears the failure after the last report rather than before it.

step0.title: Hand each notification to the scheduler
step0.text: When the upload reports progress, fails or completes, observeOn does not call the bar. It schedules a task on animationFrameScheduler that will pass that notification on.

step1.title: Wait for the next paint
step1.text: animationFrameScheduler keeps its tasks in a queue. The first task asks the browser for an animation frame; a task that arrives before that frame joins the same queue and asks for nothing more.

step2.title: Deliver the queue in order
step2.text: Just before the browser paints, the scheduler runs every task queued for that frame, oldest first. Reports that arrived between two paints reach the bar together, one after the other, and the screen shows only the last.

step3.title: An error waits its turn
step3.text: The upload's failure is one more task in the queue, so it reaches the bar after the reports before it, at the next paint. The upload's own subscription ended when it failed: observeOn changes when the bar hears, never when the upload runs.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each report, error or completion from the upload:
  schedule a task that passes it to the bar
  (the bar hears nothing yet)

if no animation frame has been requested:
  request the next one from the browser
otherwise:
  the task joins the queue for that frame

when the frame comes, just before the paint:
  run every queued task, oldest first
  (reports that arrived together are heard together)

an error is one more task in the queue:
  the bar hears it after the reports queued before it
  (the upload itself stopped when it failed)

item0.relevance: NgRx Store computes its state by passing the stream of dispatched actions through observeOn(queueScheduler) before the reducer, in modules/store/src/state.ts of the ngrx/platform repository.
item0.explanation: The State class pipes the actions through observeOn(queueScheduler), then withLatestFrom(reducer$) and scan, which folds each action into the state. queueScheduler runs a task at once unless another of its tasks is running, in which case the new task waits for that one to finish. So when code that hears a new state dispatches another action straight away, that action is reduced after the current one has been delivered rather than in the middle of it, one action at a time in the order dispatched. This is the author's reading of the pipeline from queueScheduler's documented behaviour; the file does not state its reason. item0.supports: observeOn reschedules every notification of the source, errors and completion included, on the scheduler it is given, with an optional delay; the source keeps its own scheduler; using it to split a synchronous burst is an anti-pattern, for which the scheduler belongs in the source; delay, unlike observeOn, passes errors on at once; and the page's own example observes an interval on animationFrameScheduler to update an element just before the browser repaints.

limits.item0: observeOn delivers every report; it merges none. Reports that arrive between two paints all reach the bar in one frame, so the bar is drawn more than once and only the last drawing is seen. When only the newest value per frame matters, auditTime(0, animationFrameScheduler) keeps just that one, but it treats the error differently: audit passes an error on the moment it arrives, so on this upload the failure would reach the bar before the next paint and the report waiting for that paint would never be drawn.
limits.item1: It cannot pace a synchronous burst. Had the upload produced all of {reports} at once, observeOn would queue them all before the first paint and deliver them together in it. Spreading them one per paint needs the scheduler inside the source, as scheduled(reports, animationFrameScheduler) does; observeOn only makes deliveries later, never further apart.
limits.item2: It changes when the bar hears, not when the upload runs. The upload's work, its timers and any side effect inside it keep the source's own timing and scheduler; only the hand-off downstream moves. To move the moment the source is subscribed, use subscribeOn instead.
limits.item3: A delay changes the scheduler's character. With a delay above zero, animationFrameScheduler schedules each task on a timer, as asyncScheduler would, so delivery no longer waits for a paint and every notification, the error included, is simply held that long. To shift values later, RxJS recommends delay; observeOn is for choosing the scheduler that delivers.
limits.item4: Unsubscribing cancels what is still queued. Each scheduled task belongs to the bar's subscription, so a bar torn down between a report and the next paint never hears that report.
limits.item5: A marble diagram shows the move only when the scheduler moves time. With asapScheduler, or asyncScheduler without a delay, the delivery lands in the same virtual frame as the report, so the marbles match the source's exactly although the bar hears only after the code that subscribed has finished. That order needs an ordinary asynchronous test, which is why this example uses animation frames.

item0.why: subscribeOn moves the subscription itself, so the source starts later; observeOn leaves the start alone and moves each delivery.

item1.why: delay is the tool for shifting values later in time; it passes an error on at once, where observeOn holds the error behind the values before it.

item2.why: auditTime with animationFrameScheduler keeps only the newest value per frame, where observeOn delivers every one.

item3.why: scheduled puts the scheduler inside the source, which is how a synchronous burst is spread over frames; observeOn cannot do that.

item4.why: animationFrameScheduler is the scheduler this example names: a task without a delay runs just before the next repaint, and one frame serves every task queued before it.

item5.why: queueScheduler is the scheduler NgRx Store pairs with observeOn: a task scheduled while another runs waits for it to finish.

item6.why: The rendering pattern this example follows, with auditTime as its alternative when only the last value per frame counts.

notes.0: The upload starts and the bar subscribes through observeOn. Nothing has been reported yet.
notes.1: The upload reports 10%. observeOn does not pass it on: it hands the report to animationFrameScheduler, which asks the browser for the next animation frame.
notes.2: The upload reports 30%. A frame is already requested, so the scheduler only queues this report behind the first. The bar has heard nothing.
notes.3: The browser is about to paint and runs the animation frame. The scheduler delivers both queued reports in order: the bar is drawn at 10% and at once at 30%, and only 30% reaches the screen.
notes.4: Nothing new happens. The queue is empty, and the bar shows 30% until the next report is delivered.
notes.5: The upload reports 60%. The queue is empty again, so the scheduler queues this report and requests a new frame.

intuition.text: repeat starts a finished stream over. When the source completes, repeat does not pass the completion on: it subscribes to the source again, so whatever the source does on subscription, such as sending a request, happens again. It does this a set number of times or without end, and it can wait between runs.
intuition.situation: A page waiting for a build asks the server for the build's status, waits after each answer and asks again, so the page follows the build from queued to passed without anyone pressing refresh.

example.name: A build's status, asked three times
example.description: The page reads the build's status through check$, which is cold: each subscription sends a new request, whose answer arrives {answerAfter} frames later, and then the request completes. repeat asks {checks} times and waits {wait} frames after each finished check before asking again. The answers are {answers}.

step0.title: Start the check
step0.text: When the page subscribes to status$, repeat subscribes to check$, which sends the first request, and starts counting finished runs from none.

step1.title: Pass on what the run delivers
step1.text: Each answer goes straight to the output, unchanged. An error goes straight through as well and ends the output there: repeat starts over only after a completion, never after a failure.

step2.title: Hold back the completion and count it
step2.text: When a run completes, the output does not. repeat counts the finished run, and once the count reaches {checks} it completes the output instead of going on.

step3.title: Wait, then start the check again
step3.text: Otherwise repeat starts a timer for its delay, {wait} frames here. When the timer fires it subscribes to the source again, which sends a new request, and the next run begins.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the page starts listening:
  finished = 0
  start the check

on each answer from the check:
  pass it to the page
if the check fails:
  pass the failure to the page and stop there

when the check finishes:
  finished = finished + 1
  if finished = count:
    tell the page there are no more answers

  otherwise:
    wait for the delay
    then start the check again

item0.title: RxJS API reference · repeat
item0.supports: On the source's completion repeat subscribes to it again; called with nothing it never stops, a count of zero gives an empty result, the delay may be milliseconds or a function of the repetition count, and errors are left to retry.

item1.title: RxJS API reference · RepeatConfig
item1.supports: count is unlimited when left out; delay is either a number of milliseconds or a function that is given the subscription count and returns the notifier to wait for, and a notifier that ends without a value ends the result.

item2.title: repeat.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: At the installed version the operator increments its count of finished runs before calling a delay function with it, waits on timer(delay) for a number, resubscribes only from its completion handler and gives the source no error handler of its own, and returns EMPTY without subscribing for a count of zero or less.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item3.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share, a dash for a frame, a letter for an emission, a bar for completion and a caret and an exclamation mark for the start and end of a subscription, and run mode's virtual time of one millisecond a frame, which makes the example's delay count in frames.

limits.item0: repeat starts over only after a completion. An error goes straight through and ends status$ with no new run; to try again after a failure, reach for retry, the same loop for errors.
limits.item1: A fixed count rarely fits a real poll, which should stop when the answer says so. Put takeWhile after repeat, so that the passed answer completes the output and unsubscribes the loop before another request goes out, or have a delay function return EMPTY, which completes the output instead of repeating.
limits.item2: repeat repeats only what the source does on subscription. A promise-based call made before the pipe, as in from(fetch(url)), is made once, and every repetition reads the same settled answer; wrap the call in defer so that each subscription makes it again. A hot source that has completed completes again at once, so repeating it asks for nothing new.
limits.item3: Over a source that completes as soon as it is subscribed, such as of(...), with no delay, each run starts inside the one before it. A long or endless repeat then runs out of call stack, and the output either fails with a RangeError or simply stops, neither completing nor failing. A timer delay starts each run afresh; a small count, or a take downstream, ends the loop first.
limits.item4: Each wait starts when a run completes, so the time between requests is the answer's time plus the delay, and a fixed delay never backs off: a slow or struggling server is asked as often as ever. For back-off, pass a function as delay; it is given the number of finished runs, so (finished) => timer(finished * wait) waits longer each time. For a fixed beat whatever the answers do, use timer with switchMap instead.

item0.why: Reach for retry when a run should start again after it fails: it is the same loop, subscribing again on an error where repeat does so on completion.

item1.why: Read RepeatConfig when the delay must be a function rather than a number, as back-off needs: it sets out count and delay, notifier form included.

item2.why: repeatWhen is what older code uses to say when to repeat; it is deprecated, and meeting it means rewriting it as repeat with a delay function.

item3.why: Reach for takeWhile after repeat when a poll should stop on an answer rather than after a count.

item4.why: Reach for defer when the source does its work once, at creation, such as a promise: wrapped in defer, each repetition does the work again.

item5.why: Reach for concat when the runs differ, such as one request followed by another; over a cold source, repeat with a count is concat of the source with itself.

item6.why: Reach for timer with switchMap when requests must go out on a fixed beat whatever the answers do; repeat waits for each answer before its next wait.

intuition.text: A plain Subject is a live broadcast: tune in late and what went before is gone. A ReplaySubject keeps a short recording beside the broadcast. A newcomer is played the recording first, all in one go and oldest first, and then joins the live feed, without the source being asked to run again. How much is recorded is set when the subject is made: a number of values, an age, or both.
intuition.situation: A verifier who joins a run partway through needs the latest reports to make sense of what comes next, and the run cannot be repeated for their benefit. A log that keeps the last few reports and plays them to each newcomer gives the verifier a bounded recent history in place of a rerun.

example.name: A run's report log with a late verifier
example.description: An executor posts its reports, {reports}, whether or not anyone is listening, into a log that keeps the newest {bufferSize}. A dashboard subscribes before the first report. A verifier subscribes at frame {verifierJoins}, just after tests ok has been posted, and an auditor at frame {auditorJoins}, after the run has completed.

parameters.reports: lint ok, types ok, tests ok, build ok and docs ok

step0.title: Record each value, keeping the newest few
step0.text: When the source emits, add the value to the end of the buffer. If the buffer now holds more than {bufferSize}, let the oldest go: here lint ok leaves the log when tests ok arrives.

step1.title: Pass it to everyone listening
step1.text: Every current subscriber receives the value at once, exactly as it would from a plain Subject. The buffer exists only for those who come later.

step2.title: Hand a newcomer the buffer, then go live
step2.text: When someone subscribes, add them to the listeners and immediately send them every value still in the buffer, oldest first, inside the subscribe call. The verifier, subscribing at frame {verifierJoins}, receives types ok and tests ok together, then build ok and docs ok as they are posted.

step3.title: Keep replaying after the end
step3.text: When the source completes or errors, end every current subscriber the same way but keep the buffer. Anyone who subscribes afterwards is handed the buffer and then ended at once, which is how the auditor, at frame {auditorJoins}, still sees the last reports of a finished run.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each value from the source:
  add value to the end of buffer
  if buffer holds more values than its size allows:
    let the oldest go

  send value to every current listener

when someone starts listening:
  add them to the current listeners
  send them each value in buffer, oldest first

when the source finishes or fails:
  keep buffer, and remember how the source ended
  tell every current listener the same way
  (a later listener is sent buffer, then told at once)

visual.textEquivalent: The log keeps the newest {bufferSize} reports. Frame {frame}: {now}.

item0.relevance: RxJS itself, the library this app runs on: shareReplay.ts at 7.8.2, the installed version, builds the shareReplay operator on a ReplaySubject.
item0.explanation: shareReplay is share with a ReplaySubject as the connector between a source and its subscribers. Every subscriber subscribes to that one subject, and only the subject subscribes to the source, so an expensive source such as an HTTP request runs once and a later subscriber is replayed its values instead of starting it again. The buffer size and window time pass straight to the ReplaySubject. The subject is kept after the source completes, so a completed result stays cached, but replaced after an error, so a later subscriber retries; with refCount false, the default, the source stays subscribed after the last subscriber leaves.

item4.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission, a bar completion, parentheses values emitted in the same frame with the group taking as many frames as it has characters, and a caret and an exclamation mark the start and end of a subscription.

limits.item0: Without a bound it remembers everything. new ReplaySubject() with neither a buffer size nor a window time keeps every value for as long as the subject lives, so a long-running log grows without limit and every newcomer is replayed all of it. Give it a size, an age, or both.
limits.item1: Replay arrives in one burst, inside the subscribe call. The verifier is handed {bufferSize} reports at frame {verifierJoins} before its subscribe call returns, so its handler runs for every replayed value before the line after subscribe does. Anything the handler needs must be ready before subscribing.
limits.item2: A replayed value carries no sign that it is old. The verifier cannot tell from types ok alone that it was posted before it joined. Put the time in the value when its age matters, or bound the replay with a window time, which the subject measures with the timestamp provider given to its constructor.
limits.item3: It never forgets an ending. The auditor at frame {auditorJoins} is still handed the last reports and the completion, and a subject that errored goes on replaying its buffer followed by the error. That suits the record of a finished run; to start over, make a new subject, as shareReplay does after an error but not after completion.
limits.item4: Keeping the last value is not holding a current one. A ReplaySubject that keeps one value has nothing to give a subscriber before the first value is posted, and no value to read synchronously. When there is always a current state, a BehaviorSubject says so.

item0.why: bufferSize is the bound this example sets: how many recent values a newcomer is handed.

item1.why: windowTime bounds the replay by age instead of, or as well as, by count, when a report stops mattering after a while rather than after newer ones arrive.

item2.why: A plain Subject has no memory: a newcomer hears only what is posted after it subscribes, so the verifier here would miss every report before build ok.

item3.why: BehaviorSubject is the choice when there is always a current value: it starts with one, hands a newcomer only that one, exposes it synchronously, and stops replaying after an error.

item4.why: AsyncSubject hands a newcomer only the last value, and only once the source has completed: a final result rather than a recent history.

item5.why: shareReplay puts a ReplaySubject between a source and its subscribers, so a cold source runs once and every latecomer is replayed what it produced.

intuition.text: retry is a bet that the failure was passing. It treats an error as a reason to begin again rather than an ending, and it keeps the bet out of sight: the subscriber sees the values of every attempt but none of the errors until the bet is lost. Whether beginning again means asking the server again depends on the source, not on retry.
intuition.situation: A departures board asking a server over a weak mobile connection. A request that times out often succeeds a moment later, so the board should ask again a couple of times, pausing between tries, before it tells the reader it has failed.

example.name: A departures board that asks up to three times
example.description: The board's request is defer(() => load()), so every subscription calls load() and starts a new attempt. retry allows {count} retries and waits {delay} frames before each. The first attempt times out two frames after it starts, having sent nothing. The second sends the 10:02 a frame after it starts and fails two frames later when its connection is reset. The third sends {departures} and completes.

step0.title: Start an attempt
step0.text: Subscribing calls load(), so the first attempt begins as soon as the board subscribes. Everything retry does later is another subscription to the same deferred request.

step1.title: Pass on what the attempt sends
step1.text: Each value an attempt emits goes to the board at once, whether or not that attempt fails later. retry cannot know yet, and it never takes a value back.

step2.title: On a failure with retries left, wait and ask again
step2.text: retry keeps the error from the board, counts one retry used, waits {delay} frames and subscribes again. The new attempt starts from its beginning.

step3.title: On a failure with none left, give up
step3.text: Once all {count} retries are used, the next error goes to the board and the board fails with it. Only that last error is passed on.

step4.title: Finish with the attempt that finishes
step4.text: When an attempt completes, the board completes. The errors before it were absorbed, and nothing downstream records that they happened.

pseudocode.ordinary:
retries used = 0
start an attempt

on each value from the attempt:
  pass it on
  (even if this attempt fails later)

when the attempt fails and retries used < count:
  retries used = retries used + 1
  wait delay
  start a new attempt
  (the error goes no further)

when the attempt fails and retries used = count:
  fail the output with this error

when the attempt completes:
  complete the output

limits.item0: retry repeats a subscription, not a call. It starts the work over only when subscribing starts it: an HttpClient request does, and so does a source built with defer, as the board's request is. A promise created once and wrapped with from has already failed, so every retry receives the same rejection at once and the server is never asked again.
limits.item1: A failed attempt's values stay delivered: here the 10:02 reaches the board twice. A consumer that counts, appends or acts on each value must tolerate repeats. Upstream it is worse: a write whose answer was lost may already have happened, and retrying it does it again. Retry only what is safe to repeat.
limits.item2: Every error is retried alike. A missing page or a refused request fails the same way each time, and retrying it only delays the failure by {count} waits of {delay} frames. A delay function can tell errors apart: it can return throwError for a permanent error, which then fails at once, and a timer for a transient one. A notifier that completes without emitting stops quietly instead.
limits.item3: The count covers the whole subscription unless resetOnSuccess is set. The 10:02 that the second attempt delivered did not give back the retry it used. On a long-lived feed that fails now and then, the retries run down over its life until one day the error gets through; resetOnSuccess: true restores the count whenever an attempt delivers a value.
limits.item4: Only the last error is passed on; the ones retry absorbed leave no trace, so here the timeout and the reset are invisible to the board. Report each error, in the delay function or with tap before retry, if the evidence matters. Where the reader should decide whether to try again, retry is the wrong tool: show the failure and offer a button, as this app's Tools home does with a Retry button whose press starts a fresh load.

item0.why: catchError replaces a failed source where retry starts it again. Placed after retry, it decides what the reader sees once the retries run out.

item1.why: repeat resubscribes after completion as retry does after an error: polling a request that succeeded is repeat, not retry.

item2.why: defer is what makes each subscription a new attempt, and so what gives retry something to repeat.

item3.why: retryWhen is the older, deprecated form that builds the policy from the stream of errors; code that still uses it moves to retry with a delay function.

item4.why: Retry only what is transient classifies errors before retrying, the delay-function pattern the third limit describes.

item5.why: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter grows the wait with each attempt and spreads clients apart, where this example waits the same delay every time.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, left to right. A circle is an emission, with its letter, and a bar is completion. A cross on an attempt is its error: retry keeps it from board$ and answers with a new attempt, on the next lane, {{delay}} frames later. Step the frames to follow each attempt.

notes.0: The board subscribes, and the first attempt starts.
notes.2: The first attempt fails before sending anything. retry keeps the error from the board, counts {{used}} retry used and starts to wait.
notes.3: retry is waiting out the delay. Nothing reaches the board.
notes.4: The wait is over. retry subscribes again, so load() runs again and a second attempt starts from the beginning. The board has seen no error.
notes.5: The second attempt sends the 10:02, and it goes straight to the board.
notes.7: The second attempt fails part way. Its 10:02 stays on the board. retry counts its second and last retry and waits again.
notes.8: retry waits again. The board still holds the one 10:02 it has received.
notes.9: retry subscribes a third time. If this attempt failed too, its error would reach the board.
notes.10: The third attempt starts from the beginning, so the board receives the 10:02 a second time.
notes.12: The third attempt sends the 10:15, which no earlier attempt reached.
notes.13: The third attempt completes, so the board completes. The {{failures}} errors were absorbed, and the 10:02 arrived {{repeated}} times.

intuition.text: scan lets a stream keep a running answer without anyone keeping a variable. The answer lives inside the subscription and is rebuilt from each event as it arrives, so what is shown is always the history folded so far, and no other code can change it behind the stream's back. It is reduce that reports after every step rather than once at the end, and its state belongs to the subscription that built it, not to the stream.
intuition.situation: A bank statement's balance column: each line is a deposit or a withdrawal, and the balance beside it is the one above plus that amount. The same shape fits any state built from events, such as a basket total, a score or a game's state built from commands. It goes wrong when several readers must share one balance, because each subscription keeps its own.

example.name: A statement and a phone reading one account
example.description: A bank's live feed sends the amounts {amounts} at frames 1, 4 and 8 and completes at frame 11. The balance stream folds them into a balance that opens at {opening}. A statement subscribes to it from the start; a phone app subscribes to the same stream at frame 5, after the first two amounts have gone by.

step0.title: Start each subscriber from the seed
step0.text: When something subscribes, scan gives that subscription its own state, set to the seed: the opening of {opening}. Nothing is sent yet. The phone, subscribing at frame 5, starts from the opening too, not from the balance the statement has reached.

step1.title: Fold each amount into the state
step1.text: When an amount arrives, each subscription's reducer receives that subscription's state and the amount, and its result replaces the state. Without a seed, the first amount would become the state unchanged and the reducer would first run on the second.

step2.title: Send the new state
step2.text: The new state goes out at once, on every amount, so the statement's balance column fills line by line. reduce would keep the same state but send only the last one, when the feed completes.

step3.title: Finish with the feed
step3.text: When the feed completes, each balance stream completes and sends nothing more. An error from the feed, or one the reducer throws, ends the stream with that error, and the state goes with the subscription.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a reader starts listening:
  give that reader its own balance, set to the opening
  (a reader who starts late still starts from the opening)
  send nothing yet

on each amount from the feed, for each reader:
  if the reader has no balance yet (no opening was given):
    balance = amount
  otherwise:
    balance = balance + amount

  send the reader's new balance

when the feed finishes:
  finish each reader's balances
  (the last balance has already been sent)
if the feed fails, or the addition throws:
  fail the reader's balances with that error
