limits.item0: Each subscription folds on its own, and nothing warns a late one. The phone subscribes at frame 5, starts from the opening and ends on a balance the account never had. When several readers need one running state, fold once and share it: shareReplay(1) after scan gives a late subscriber the current balance at once, and NgRx and this app's scene facade push each state into a BehaviorSubject.
limits.item1: The seed is one value shared by every subscription. A reducer that mutates an object or array seed, rather than returning a new state, changes the seed itself, so the next subscription or a retry starts from the mutated state. Return a new state from the reducer.
limits.item2: Without a seed, the first value becomes the state unchanged and the reducer first runs on the second value, with index 1. That is right only when a value already is a state: leaving out the opening here would take the first deposit for the whole balance. At the installed version a seed of undefined passed explicitly still counts as a seed, because scan counts its arguments.
limits.item3: scan never sends the seed. The statement is blank until the first amount, and the phone shows nothing from subscribing until the next amount arrives. Add startWith(opening) after scan when a fresh fold must show its starting balance at once.
limits.item4: The reducer must be synchronous and should be pure. A reducer that needs a request for each value belongs in mergeScan or switchScan. One with side effects repeats them for every subscription, since each subscription runs its own fold.

item0.why: reduce is the same fold when only the final balance matters: it sends once, when the source completes.

item1.why: mergeScan is the choice when computing the next state needs a stream, such as a request per value; each inner result becomes the next state.

item2.why: switchScan is mergeScan that cancels the computation still in flight when the next value arrives, so only the newest one becomes the state.

item3.why: shareReplay is how several readers share one fold, so a late subscriber receives the current balance instead of starting a new fold from the seed.

item4.why: A BehaviorSubject holds the current state where other code reads it or subscribes late; a folded stream often feeds one, as in NgRx.

item5.why: startWith puts the seed on screen before the first value, which scan itself never does.

notes.0: The statement subscribes. scan holds the opening, {{opening}}, as its state and sends nothing: no amount has arrived yet.
notes.1: A deposit of {{deposit}} arrives. scan adds it to the {{opening}} it holds, keeps the result and sends it: the statement shows {{balance}}.
notes.4: A withdrawal of {{withdrawal}} arrives. The state is now {{before}}, not the opening, so the statement shows {{balance}}.
notes.5: The phone subscribes to the same balance stream. scan starts a separate fold for it from the opening, {{opening}}; the deposit and the withdrawal before this frame are not replayed to it.
notes.8: A deposit of {{deposit}} reaches both folds. The statement adds it to {{before}} and shows {{balance}}; the phone adds it to {{opening}} and shows {{phone}}, a balance the account never had.
notes.11: The feed completes, and both balances complete with nothing more sent: each last balance went out at frame 8.

intuition.text: Where share is a live broadcast, shareReplay is a broadcast with a recording of its last moments: whoever tunes in late hears the recording first and then the live sound, so no reader ever starts empty. The recording is what it costs. To keep it current the source goes on running after the last listener has gone, and a broadcast that has finished is kept and never run again.
intuition.situation: The page of the share study: a stock quote polled from the server, shown in a tile from the start and in a chart the user opens later. Here the chart must draw the current quote the moment it opens rather than sit empty until the next poll, and the question becomes what that convenience costs once the user has left.

example.name: The quote page, with the latest quote kept
example.description: The streams are those of the share study: a poll that fetches a quote every {pollEvery} frames, the first one frame after it starts; the tile subscribing at frame 0; the chart opening at frame {chartOpensAt}; and the user leaving at frame {leftAt}, which unsubscribes both readers. The quote is shared with shareReplay(1), a memory of {bufferSize} quote with refCount left false.

step0.title: Start one run and a memory for the first reader
step0.text: When the tile subscribes, shareReplay creates a memory that holds the latest {bufferSize} quote and subscribes to the poll, once, to fill it. The readers listen to the memory, not to the poll.

step1.title: Store each value, then pass it on
step1.text: Each quote goes into the memory, pushing out the oldest once the memory is full, and on to every reader present at that moment.

step2.title: Replay the memory to a late reader
step2.text: The chart subscribes at frame {chartOpensAt} and is handed the quote in the memory in that same frame, then the live quotes alongside the tile. The memory holds {bufferSize} quote, so that is all the chart is given before the live ones.

step3.title: Keep running when the readers leave
step3.text: At frame {leftAt} both readers unsubscribe. With refCount false, as shareReplay(1) leaves it, having no reader stops nothing: the poll goes on sending requests and filling the memory for no one. With refCount: true it would stop here, and the memory would be dropped with it.

step4.title: Keep a completed run, forget a failed one
step4.text: Had the poll completed, the memory would keep its quote and the completion, and every later reader would receive both at once with no new request. When it fails, the readers present receive the error and end, the memory is dropped, and the next reader starts a new poll with nothing to replay.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the first reader arrives:
  make a memory that holds the latest quote
  start the poll, once, feeding the memory

on each quote from the poll:
  put it in the memory, pushing the older one out
  give it to every reader present at that moment

when a later reader arrives:
  give it the quote in the memory straight away
  then the live quotes, as every other reader gets them

when a reader leaves:
  remove it from the readers present
  (with no reader left the poll keeps running
   and keeps filling the memory, for no one)

when the poll completes:
  keep the memory and the completion: a later reader gets the stored
  quote and the completion at once, and nothing is fetched again
when the poll fails:
  give the failure to every reader present and forget the memory:
  the next reader to arrive is a first reader again

limits.item0: The default never lets go. After frame {leftAt} the poll goes on fetching for no one, and it will do so for as long as the app runs, because shareReplay(1) leaves refCount false. On a stream that belongs to a page or a component, write shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }), which stops the poll with the last reader. Keep the default for a value that should stay warm for the whole application, owned by a long-lived service that can end it.
limits.item1: refCount: true gives up the cache along with the leak. The memory is dropped together with the poll, so a reader who returns after everyone has left starts a new poll and waits for its first quote, exactly as with share. To keep the last quote through a short absence and still stop the poll in the end, use share with a ReplaySubject connector and a delayed resetOnRefCountZero.
limits.item2: A completed source is cached for good. Had the quote been a single request that completed before the chart opened, the chart would receive the stored quote and the completion at once, and the request would never be sent again: there is no invalidation and no expiry. A value that must be refreshed needs a trigger to rebuild from, a refresh stream switched to a new request, with shareReplay after the switch.
limits.item3: Only the newest values are replayed, and they are as old as their fetch. The chart receives the second quote, not the first, and shows it as current although it was fetched before the chart opened. A larger buffer replays more; shareReplay() with no size keeps every value for the life of the stream; and windowTime refuses to replay a value older than the window.
limits.item4: An error is neither kept nor retried. When the poll fails, the readers present receive the error and end, the memory is discarded, and the next reader starts a new poll with nothing to replay. To keep the readers through a failed request, retry before shareReplay, inside the shared part.

item0.why: share is the choice when a late reader can wait for the next value, or when the work must stop with the last reader and start afresh for the next: it keeps no memory and resets on every ending by default.

item1.why: ShareReplayConfig, the object form, is the only way to set refCount: true, and refCount is required there, so writing it out turns the leak trade-off into a visible decision.

item2.why: A ReplaySubject on its own is the choice when the app pushes the values itself rather than sharing a source; as share's connector it gives the same memory with each reset chosen separately.

item3.why: BehaviorSubject is the choice when there is a sensible value before the first fetch, such as a placeholder, so that no reader ever starts empty, or when the app writes the state itself instead of polling it.

item4.why: This analysis is the one to reach for when auditing an app for subscriptions that outlive their views: it names the default refCount as a leak source and the fixes for it.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. A circle is an emission, with its letter. quote$ is the poll; tile$ and chart$ are its two readers, and each lane starts where that reader subscribes. A reader's lane ends in a small ring where it left the page; the poll's lane runs on. Step the frames to follow each quote.

intuition.text: One run of the source, for whoever is listening. share stands between a source and its readers: the first reader to arrive starts the source, every later reader joins that same run at the point it has reached, and when the last reader leaves, share stops the source and forgets it, so the next reader starts it over. While anyone listens the stream is hot, and a reader who arrives late has missed what came before; with no one listening it is cold again.
intuition.situation: A page polls a stock quote and shows it twice: in a tile that is there from the start and in a chart the user opens later. Every subscription to an HttpClient call issues a request of its own, so two readers would run two polls. They should share one, and it should stop when the user leaves the page.

example.name: A quote tile and a chart opened later
example.description: The page polls a quote every {pollEvery} frames, the first arriving one frame after the poll starts. The tile subscribes at frame 0; the user opens the chart at frame {chartOpensAt}, between the second and third quotes, and leaves the page at frame {leftAt}, which unsubscribes both readers. The poll never completes on its own. The shareReplay study runs exactly these streams, so the two diagrams differ only in the operator.

step0.title: Start one run for the first reader
step0.text: When the tile subscribes and nothing is running, share subscribes to the poll, once. Every reader that follows listens to this run; none of them starts a poll of its own.

step1.title: Pass each value to the readers present
step1.text: Each quote goes to every reader subscribed at that moment, and share keeps no copy of it.

step2.title: A late reader joins where the run stands
step2.text: The chart subscribes at frame {chartOpensAt}, into the running poll. share has nothing stored to hand it, so the chart stays empty until the next quote arrives for both readers.

step3.title: Stop when the last reader leaves
step3.text: share counts its readers. When the count falls to none, at frame {leftAt} here, it unsubscribes from the poll and forgets it: no further request is sent, and the next reader to arrive starts a new poll as if share had never run.

step4.title: Forget the run when it ends
step4.text: If the poll completes or fails, share passes the completion or the error to the readers present, which ends them, and forgets the run, so the next reader starts a new one. This is a reset, not a retry: the readers who were there have already ended.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the first reader arrives:
  start the poll, once, for every reader to come

on each quote from the poll:
  give it to every reader present at that moment
  (store nothing: a reader who arrives later never sees it)

when a later reader arrives:
  add it to the readers present
  (it waits for the next quote; nothing is replayed)

when a reader leaves:
  remove it from the readers present
  if none is left:
    stop the poll and forget it
    (the next reader to arrive is a first reader again)

when the poll completes or fails:
  pass that on to every reader present, which ends them
  forget the poll: the next reader to arrive is a first reader again
  (nothing is retried for the readers who were there)

limits.item0: A late reader starts empty. The chart opened at frame {chartOpensAt} has nothing to draw until the next quote, and the quotes fetched before it opened never reach it. limits.item1: Every reset repeats the work. Once the last reader has gone, or the source has completed or failed, the next reader starts the source again. limits.item2: A reset is not a retry. If the poll fails, the tile and the chart both receive the error and stop; only a reader that subscribes afterwards starts a new poll. intuition.text: Of the subjects, this is the one with no memory. It keeps a list of who is listening and whether it has ended, and nothing else: a value exists only in the instant it is pushed, so whoever is on the list then hears it and whoever arrives later never will. Subscribing costs nothing and starts nothing; the work that produces the values happens once, outside the subject, however many listen.
intuition.situation: The scene's Step button, heard by two parts of the page: the painter, which redraws on every step, and a step log opened partway through. example.name: A Step button, a log opened late and a latecomer
example.description: The Step button is pressed three times, {presses}, at frames 2, 6 and 10, and the page closes at frame 14, which ends the presses. Every press goes into one subject. The painter listens from frame 0, the step log subscribes at frame {logOpensAt}, between the first press and the second, and a summary panel subscribes at frame {latecomerArrivesAt}, after the page has closed. In the app a press calls next on the subject; here the presses are an input stream the subject subscribes to, which makes the same calls.

step0.title: Feed the subject once
step0.text: The subject is subscribed to the presses a single time. However many parts of the page listen, each press is produced once and goes into the subject once; a cold stream would instead run its work again for every subscriber.

step1.title: Put each listener on the list
step1.text: Subscribing adds the listener to the subject's list and does nothing else: no work starts for it, and nothing earlier is replayed, because nothing earlier was kept. The log, which subscribes at frame {logOpensAt}, has missed press 1 for good. A listener that arrives after the end is told of the end instead, at once.

step2.title: Hand each value to everyone on the list
step2.text: When a press arrives, the subject hands it to each listener on its list at that moment, one after another within the same frame, so the painter and the log both hear press 2 in the frame it is pressed. The press is not kept once it has been handed round.

step3.title: End everyone together
step3.text: When the presses complete, or fail with an error, the subject passes that ending to every listener, empties its list and stays closed, so a later press would be ignored. The summary panel, subscribing at frame {latecomerArrivesAt}, is told at once that it is over and hears no press.

steps holds a list of listeners and whether it has ended, and no values
connect steps to the presses, once

when a part of the page starts listening to steps:
  if steps has ended: pass on that ending at once, and add nothing
  otherwise: add the listener to the list
  (nothing is replayed: no earlier press was kept)

when a press arrives:
  for each listener on the list at this moment:
    hand it the press
  keep nothing of the press

when the presses end, normally or with an error:
  pass that ending to every listener on the list
  empty the list, and remember that steps has ended
  ignore any press that comes later

limits.item0: A Subject remembers nothing. A listener that subscribes late has missed everything before it, as the log misses press 1, and one that subscribes after the end hears only the ending, as the summary panel does. When a late listener needs how things stand rather than what happens next, use a BehaviorSubject; when it needs the last few events, a ReplaySubject with a bounded buffer.
limits.item1: Handing out the subject itself lets any listener call next, error or complete for everyone, so one consumer's complete ends the stream for all the others. Keep it private and expose asObservable, with methods for pushing, as the scene clock does with tick.
limits.item2: A completed or errored subject stays closed: later next calls are dropped without a word, so something that is created again needs a new subject. limits.item3: Delivery is synchronous and in subscription order. A listener that pushes into the same subject from inside its handler starts a nested round of delivery, so the listeners after it hear the new value before the one it was answering.
limits.item4: A hand-wired subject is state someone must own. Where a creation function already says it, such as fromEvent for a DOM event or from for a promise, prefer it; to share one execution of an existing observable, share makes and manages the subject itself. A subject earns its place where ordinary code pushes values in, as the scene facade's step method does through the clock's tick.

item2.why: ReplaySubject keeps a bounded number of recent values and replays them to late subscribers, for a listener that needs some of what it missed.

item4.why: share creates and manages the subject when the aim is to share one execution of an existing observable among its subscribers.

item5.why: Subjects as public API is the rule behind keeping the subject private and exposing asObservable.

item0.explanation: In its constructor the facade merges the clock's ticks with the commands the page sends, folds them into the current run with scan, and ends the pipe with takeUntilDestroyed given the DestroyRef it injected. When whatever provides the facade is destroyed, that notifier fires, the fold completes and the facade's subscription to the clock's ticks and to its commands is released; a separate onDestroy callback pauses the clock itself. takeUntilDestroyed is the last operator in the pipe, so no operator after it keeps a subscription of its own.

item1.relevance: Angular's rxjs-interop package, @angular/core/rxjs-interop, from which this app imports takeUntilDestroyed and toSignal, defines the operator in take_until_destroyed.ts of the angular/angular repository.
item1.explanation: The operator builds its notifier from a DestroyRef, the one passed in or the current injection context's: an observable that emits when the DestroyRef's onDestroy callbacks run, or emits at once if it is already destroyed, and whose teardown unregisters the callback. It then returns source.pipe(takeUntil(destroyed$)). The early emission meets the first step of this study: takeUntil listens to the notifier first, so a stream piped through an already-destroyed context is never subscribed. The file is pinned to the commit read on 2026-10-31.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · takeUntil
item0.supports: The operator's documented contract: the output follows the source up to the notifier's first value and then completes, while a notifier that completes without any value leaves every source value passing.

item1.title: takeUntil.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version the notifier is subscribed before the source, and the source only if the output is still open after that; the notifier's next handler completes the output and its complete handler does nothing.

item2.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item2.supports: Defines the notation the diagram and its spec are written in: one dash for each frame of virtual time, a bar for completion, a caret marking frame zero of a hot observable, where the test subscribes, and in a subscriptions string a caret and an exclamation mark where a subscription begins and is unsubscribed.

item3.title: eslint-plugin-rxjs · no-unsafe-takeuntil
item3.supports: The rule flags takeUntil placed ahead of operators that subscribe to further streams, such as combineLatest, because those subscriptions can outlive the notifier; its correct example moves takeUntil to the end of the pipe.

limits.item0: takeUntil ends only what comes before it. An operator placed after it that subscribes to streams of its own, such as switchMap or combineLatest, keeps those subscriptions alive when the notifier fires, so the leak takeUntil was meant to prevent remains. Put it last in the pipe, as the scene facade does.
limits.item1: Letting go is not stopping the work. Here the shared clock keeps ticking after the page closes and the page simply hears none of it, which is right for a clock other pages use; whether a producer stops when its last listener leaves depends on that producer's own teardown, not on takeUntil.
limits.item2: The output completes, which is a notification downstream code will act on. A complete handler or finalize runs when the page closes, so code that treats completion as the work being finished, rather than abandoned, misreads a close as a success.
limits.item3: The notifier must actually emit while the page listens. A closed signal that only completes, such as a Subject someone completes without calling next, stops nothing; so does a plain Subject that emitted before the page started listening, as when a late subscription is made after the page's destroy signal has fired; and one that never fires leaves the subscription open for as long as the source runs. A notifier that fails fails the output with its error.

item0.why: takeUntilDestroyed is Angular's packaged form of this study, with the notifier built from a DestroyRef; it is what this app's scene facade uses.

item1.why: The anti-pattern of placing takeUntil before a subscribing operator, the first of the limits here, with the lint rule that catches it.

item2.why: The leak takeUntil exists to prevent: a subscription to a source that never completes lives until something ends it.

item3.why: Complete is not cancellation: takeUntil turns a stop into a completion that downstream sees, which a bare unsubscribe never sends.

item4.why: take bounds a subscription by a count of values rather than by an outside event; takeWhile, rxc:193, bounds it by a test of each value.

item5.why: skipUntil is the mirror image: it ignores values until a notifier emits and passes them afterwards.

notes.0: The page opens. takeUntil subscribes to closed$ first and then to the clock.
notes.2: The clock ticks and the page shows the tick.
notes.7: The page closes and closed$ emits. takeUntil completes the output and, in the same frame, unsubscribes from the clock and from closed$.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. A circle is an emission, with its letter, and a bar is completion. The small ring that ends the tick$ lane is where this page let go of the clock, not where the clock stopped: the clock ticks on for its other listeners, which this drawing does not show. The ring on closed$ is where takeUntil stopped listening to the signal it had just heard. Step the frames to follow each tick.

intuition.text: timeout is a deadline on silence, not on duration. Its clock starts when it subscribes and starts again with every value, so a slow source that keeps talking passes and a quick one that goes quiet fails. When the clock runs out it stops listening before it reports the failure, so a page the server sends after the deadline, page 4 here, never reaches the reader.
intuition.situation: A request to a server that may hang. Without a deadline a stalled request leaves a spinner turning for ever; with one, the page can say that the request failed and offer Retry.

example.name: A report that stalls
example.description: A slow server sends a report in pages, and a frame here is a virtual millisecond. pages$ allows {startup} frames for the first page, because the server needs time to start a report, and {gap} frames between pages after that. The first page comes just inside the startup wait and {pagesShown} pages arrive in time; then the server stalls, the gap wait runs out and pages$ fails with a TimeoutError.

step0.title: Start the startup wait
step0.text: When pages$ is subscribed, listen to the report and start a timer for the startup wait. Had no first wait been given, the gap wait would time the first page too.

step1.title: Start the wait again on each page
step1.text: A page that arrives before the timer runs out is passed on at once, counted and kept as the last page. The timer is cancelled and started again for the gap wait, so each deadline is measured from the previous page, not from the start of the report.

step2.title: Give up when a wait runs out
step2.text: If the timer runs out first, stop listening to the report, which also forgets the last page, and fail pages$ with a TimeoutError whose info counts the pages seen. Given a with factory instead, timeout passes the factory the same info and switches to the stream it returns rather than failing.

step3.title: Stand down when the report ends
step3.text: If the report completes or fails before a timer runs out, cancel the timer and pass the completion or failure on.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the reader starts listening for pages:
  listen to the report
  start a timer for the startup wait
    (or for the gap wait when no startup wait is given)

on each page from the report:
  cancel the timer
  pass the page on
  count it and keep it as the last page
  start a timer for the gap wait

when the timer runs out:
  stop listening to the report
    (which forgets the last page)
  tell the reader the report timed out
    (with the count of pages seen)

when the report completes or fails:
  cancel the timer
  pass the completion or failure on

item0.relevance: Where this app uses it: libs/shared/data-access/src/lib/interceptors.ts puts a timeout on the stream of events of every HTTP request.
item0.explanation: timeoutInterceptor reads a duration from the request's context, falling back to the environment's requestTimeoutMs, and pipes the request through timeout({ each: duration }). With each alone the same wait times the first event and every gap after it. Angular's fetch backend, HttpClient's default, emits a Sent event as soon as it starts the request and before it awaits the response, so in practice the wait runs from Sent to the response, and from one progress event to the next when progress is reported: a slow download that keeps arriving is not cut off, and a stalled one is. When the wait runs out, timeout unsubscribes, and the fetch backend's teardown aborts the unfinished request.

item1.relevance: NgRx Data is the NgRx library that keeps entity collections in sync with a REST back end; DefaultDataService, in modules/data/src/dataservices/default-data.service.ts of the ngrx/platform repository, makes each collection's HTTP calls.
item1.explanation: When its configuration sets a timeout in milliseconds, execute() pipes each HttpClient call through timeout(this.timeout + this.saveDelay), a bare number and so a wait between values, and then through catchError, which wraps whatever failed, the TimeoutError included, in a DataServiceError. HttpClient's calls emit only the response unless a caller asks for events, so here the one wait runs from subscription to the response and bounds the whole request; the app's interceptor, which sees the Sent event first, measures from Sent instead. The file is pinned to the 22.0.1 release commit read on 2026-10-31.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · timeout
item0.supports: first times only the arrival of the first value, from subscription or until a Date; each times the wait between values, and times the first value too when first is not given; without a with factory the operator fails with a TimeoutError, which the page suggests telling apart with instanceof, and with one it switches to the stream the factory returns.

item1.title: timeout.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version each value cancels the timer and starts it again for each; when a timer runs out the operator unsubscribes from its source, whose teardown sets the last value to null, and only then builds the info of meta, seen and lastValue for the with factory or the TimeoutError; with no each, no timer follows the first value; meta comes from the operator's configuration; and TimeoutError's documentation recommends a project's own error class over building or subclassing it.

item2.title: Angular guide · Making HTTP requests, Timeouts
item2.supports: HttpClient has its own timeout option, a number of milliseconds after which the backend request is aborted and an error emitted, covering the backend request alone and not the interceptor chain; such a timeout reaches the caller as an HttpErrorResponse of status 0 whose error is a DOMException named TimeoutError.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item3.supports: In run mode the TestScheduler is used automatically by operators that use the AsyncScheduler, as timeout does by default, and one frame is one virtual millisecond, so the spec's frames stand for the waits' milliseconds.

item4.title: ReactiveX/rxjs issue 7324 · TimeoutInfo.lastValue is null when it shouldn't be
item4.supports: A lastValue of null in the info a timeout hands to its with factory, whatever the source emitted before the wait ran out, was reported against RxJS 7.8.1; the issue was closed as not planned on 2026-07-22, without a fix.

item5.title: fetch.ts in Angular v22.2.3
item5.supports: Angular's fetch backend emits the Sent event before it awaits the response, emits download progress events when progress is reported, aborts an unfinished request when it is unsubscribed, and implements a request's own timeout option by aborting the request when that time has passed.

item6.title: backend.ts in Angular v22.2.3
item6.supports: HttpBackend is provided in root as the fetch backend, so the fetch backend is what HttpClient uses unless an application configures another.

item7.title: client.ts in Angular v22.2.3
item7.supports: Unless a call asks to observe events, HttpClient filters the request's event stream down to the response before handing it to the caller.

limits.item0: A timeout stops listening; it does not undo work. When the wait runs out, timeout unsubscribes from its source, and what follows is up to the source: Angular's fetch backend aborts the request, a promise-based call runs on unheard, and a server that has already received a save may still apply it. Retrying a timed-out write can apply it twice.
limits.item1: Each wait measures silence, not total time. A source that keeps sending a value just inside the gap wait never times out, however long it runs. For a budget on the whole request, takeUntil with a timer ends it quietly, or HttpClient's own timeout option aborts the backend request; that option fails with an HttpErrorResponse whose error is a DOMException named TimeoutError, which an instanceof check against RxJS's TimeoutError does not catch.
limits.item2: With each alone, the first value is held to the same wait; with first alone, nothing is timed after the first value. In this example the gap wait alone fails pages$ before the server has sent its first page, and the startup wait alone never reports the stall.
limits.item3: The error does not name the wait that ran out, and it does not keep the last value. Its info has a lastValue field, but at RxJS 7.8.2 the operator has set it to null by the time it builds the info, so a handler that needs the last page must keep it itself, with tap for instance. The count of values seen is right: a count of zero means the first wait ran out. meta is fixed when the operator is configured, so it can name the request but not the wait.
limits.item4: A timeout is an error, and an error ends the stream. To show it and offer Retry, follow timeout with catchError; to fall back to other values instead, give timeout a with factory.

item0.why: TimeoutError is what timeout fails with. Check for it with instanceof; RxJS recommends a project's own error class for a timeout of its own.

item1.why: TimeoutInfo is what the error and the with factory receive: meta, the count of values seen, and a lastValue that at RxJS 7.8.2 is already null when a wait runs out.

item2.why: catchError turns the TimeoutError into a failure the page can show and offer Retry for.

item3.why: retry subscribes again after a timeout, which sends the request again: right for a read, risky for a write the server may already have applied.

item4.why: timeoutWith was the way to switch to a fallback on timeout; it is deprecated in favour of timeout's with option.

item5.why: takeUntil with a timer is a budget on the whole stream that ends it quietly instead of failing it.

item6.why: debounceTime also measures silence, but it waits for silence and then emits, where timeout treats silence as a failure.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, one virtual millisecond each. A circle is a page, with its letter, and a cross is an error. report$ ends in a small hollow ring where timeout stopped listening to the server, and pages$ ends on the same frame in a cross, the TimeoutError it fails with. Step the frames to follow each wait.

notes.0: The report is requested and the startup wait begins. It is the longer wait, because the server needs time to start a report.
notes.4: Had the first page been held to the gap wait, it would have run out here, before the server answered. The startup wait is still running.
notes.5: The first page arrives inside the startup wait and is shown. The timer starts again, now for the shorter gap wait.
notes.8: The second page arrives inside its gap and is shown. The timer starts again from here, not from the start of the report.
notes.10: The third page arrives sooner still and is shown. The timer starts again.
notes.14: No page has come within a gap of the third. timeout stops listening to the server and fails pages$ with a TimeoutError that counts the pages seen; its record of the last page is already empty.
